result:
The final answer $(k+1)(n-1)-1$ is correct. The upper bound and the construction both check out.

**Upper bound.** Each spanning tree of a subgraph $H$ has $|V(H)|-1$ edges, so $\tau(H)\ge k+1$ forces $|E(H)|\ge (k+1)(|V(H)|-1)$. The converse direction, that $\gamma_f(G)\ge k+1$ implies a subgraph with $k+1$ edge-disjoint spanning trees, follows from Nash-Williams–Tutte applied to a densest subgraph $H_0$. For any partition $P$ of $V(H_0)$ into $p$ parts, $e_{H_0}(P)\ge \gamma_f(p-1)\ge (k+1)(p-1)$. So $\tau_k$-maximality forces $\gamma_f(G)<k+1$, hence $|E(G)|<(k+1)(n-1)$.

**Construction.** Start with $K_{2k+2}-e$, which has $(k+1)(2k+1)-1$ edges. It has no $k+1$ edge-disjoint spanning trees, since it has fewer than $(k+1)(2k+1)$ edges. Repeatedly add a vertex joined to $k+1$ existing vertices. Induction shows every subgraph $H$ satisfies $|E(H)|\le (k+1)(|V(H)|-1)-1$. The small cases (one-vertex and two-vertex subgraphs) are fine since $k\ge 10$. So the graph on $n$ vertices has $(k+1)(n-1)-1$ edges and no $k+1$ edge-disjoint spanning trees.

**Saturation.** Adding any non-edge gives $(k+1)(n-1)$ edges. The whole graph then has density $\ge k+1$, so by the claim it contains $k+1$ edge-disjoint spanning trees.

As a sanity check, for $k+1=2$ the formula gives $2n-3$, which matches the known extremal value for graphs without two edge-disjoint spanning trees.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
